articles.title: Dem’s data center attack in critical Senate race hits snag when money trail surfaces: 'Jekyll-and-Hyde'
articles.summary: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown accepted $20,000 from Google's PAC while running ads attacking a Google data center in Lancaster, Ohio.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is targeting Republican Sen. Jon Husted over Ohio's growing data center industry in a new campaign ad that features a facility owned by Google — whose corporate PAC and lobbyists have contributed thousands of dollars to Brown's campaigns. The Sept. 4 ad features an Ohioan blaming Husted for spearheading "the push to bring data centers to Ohio" and linking their expansion to "higher electric bills." The facility featured in the ad, which opened in Lancaster in 2023, is owned by Google. Campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Google's corporate PAC contributed $20,000 to Brown over his political career. Brown also received thousands of dollars from individuals who lobby for Google, including two whose firms have worked on permitting, grid reliability and energy affordability issues. WATCH: GOP SENATOR UNLOADS ON 'CREATURE OF WASHINGTON' CHALLENGER IN CRITICAL SENATE SHOWDOWN "Apparently Google is terrible enough to put in a campaign attack ad, but perfectly acceptable when the political contributions are coming in," Mehek Cooke, a GOP strategist and attorney in Ohio, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "That is the contradiction Brown needs to answer. If Google’s Lancaster investment is so bad for Ohio, why was Google political money acceptable to Sherrod Brown?" Among the contributors are Google lobbyist Lisa Kountoupes, who donated $3,500 in March, and Google lobbyist Michael D. Smith, who donated a total of $10,200 to Brown since 2017, according to Federal Election Commission records. The contributions were made to Friends of Sherrod Brown, Brown's principal campaign committee. Kountoupes’s firm, Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid, was hired by Google in December to lobby on "issues related to permitting reform" tied to the company's data center needs, Politico previously reported. Smith's firm, Cornerstone Government Affairs, reported lobbying for Google on "issues related to permitting reform for grid reliability and energy affordability," according to federal lobbying filings. FEC records show Brown also received a combined $6,000 over the past decade from three additional Google lobbyists. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Lauren Chou, a spokeswoman for Brown's campaign, highlighted Brown's opposition to Ohio's data center expansion, saying Husted "led the charge," but did not address Brown's past campaign contributions. "Husted is a ‘chief reason’ Ohio has 226 data centers and is ‘the face of data centers’ in Ohio," Chou wrote. "Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to subsidize these costs and Ohioans – not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends – should get to decide if data centers are built in their community." Cooke accused Brown of acting like his "Google relationship in Washington does not count," calling it "Jekyll-and-Hyde politics." FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE "For nearly five decades, Brown has sold himself as the plaid-shirt, working-class populist," she said. "He lost in 2024, and now he is back running the same playbook: say one thing to Ohioans while his Washington record tells a very different story." Brown, who is seeking to return to the U.S. Senate in the high-stakes race against Husted, was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006 before losing his reelection bid in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. But this isn’t the first time Brown’s comeback campaign has faced questions over conflicting positions. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE In 2015, Brown celebrated the construction of an Amazon data center in central Ohio, saying in a press release the new facility "is great news for New Albany and central Ohio." Despite his public praise, Brown has become an outspoken critic of Ohio's growing number of data centers, a defining issue in Ohio politics ahead of the midterms. President Donald Trump has pushed to expand the facilities, warning that communities that block them would "end up being backwards and poor." But Cooke said this about more than one local data center. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "America is in a global race for AI, computing capacity and energy infrastructure," she said. "China is not slowing down because American politicians discovered that attacking data centers makes a convenient campaign commercial." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Husted campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said that Brown failed Ohio families during his 32 years in Washington and is "once again resorting to lies instead of facing his abysmal record head-on. " "The House overwhelmingly passed Sen. Husted’s bipartisan legislation requiring data center companies to pay for the power they use, but Senate Democrats blocked it," Natoce said. "Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution. It’s despicable."

articles.title: Iowa has become tricky territory for GOP in midterm election homestretch
articles.summary: Iowa Republicans are being presented with the difficult choice of embracing President Trump in the final stretch of the midterms as Democrats seek to tie them to the administration. The dynamic was on full display in Council Bluffs on Friday, when Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn joined Vice President Vance on the campaign trail, but…
articles.body:
Iowa Republicans are being presented with the difficult choice of embracing President Trump in the final stretch of the midterms as Democrats seek to tie them to the administration.

The dynamic was on full display in Council Bluffs on Friday, when Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn joined Vice President Vance on the campaign trail, but Republican Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson opted to skip the event.

Hawkeye State Republicans are acutely aware of the risks of siding with the administration on issues like the Iran war.

Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) and Zach Nunn (R) were among a group of seven House Republicans who voted with Democrats this week to block Trump from continuing the Iran war without approval from Congress.

All eyes were on the state’s Republican gubernatorial and Senate campaigns Friday with the vice president in town.

Hinson’s campaign cited scheduling conflicts ahead of the rally, but Vance still gave her a shoutout at the beginning of the event.

“I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson for United States Senator from the great state of Iowa?” Vance said, eliciting applause from the crowd.

Vance went on to tout Lahn’s candidacy before launching into a roughly seven-minute attack on Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand.

“The choice is this simple. It’s common sense versus crazy. It’s a man who listens to you versus a man who looks down on you. It’s a governor who fights for you versus a governor who fights against you,” Vance said.

“You have an opportunity to send not just Rob Sand but the entire Democrat Party a message: Check the crazy at the door, and learn to fight for Americans for a change,” he continued.

Polls show both races tightening, with Democrats holding a slight edge.

A poll released earlier this month from Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media shows Sand leading Lahn 49 percent to 46 percent. The same poll found Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek leading Hinson 46 percent to 44 percent.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the Senate race as a “toss up” and the gubernatorial race as “lean Democratic.”

Hinson has shown other signs she is carefully navigating how to approach Trump and the administration in her race. Hinson attended last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, but unlike other high-profile Republicans in attendance, she did not speak on stage.

“Zach Lahn and Ashley Hinson are two very different candidates, and they’re also facing two very different opponents,” said one Republican operative familiar with Iowa.

Lahn had strong support from the “Make American Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement in the Republican primary, scoring a major primary victory against Trump-backed candidate Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa).

Sand holds a fundraising and cash-on-hand advantage over Lahn. Many Republicans, including Vance, have hit Sand over receiving high-dollar contributions from family members.

Sand’s campaign fired back at Vance and Lahn in a statement, accusing the vice president of bailing the Republican nominee out.

“He’s bringing in another D.C. insider to try to bail him out because he can’t answer for his frequent flights to Kansas or his decade-long career as a political operative,” said Maddie Moher, Sand’s campaign press secretary.

“The attacks Lahn has pushed have been repeatedly found false by independent fact-checkers and news outlets, and outsourcing his talking points to another Washington politician doesn’t make them true. Iowa voters know the leader who will actually show up and work for them is Rob Sand,” she continued.

Miller-Meeks and Nunn were not in attendance at Friday’s rally, which did not take place in either of their congressional districts.

However, the pair made headlines along with five other Republicans for voting with Democrats on a war powers resolution earlier this week that would have curbed Trump’s power in continuing the war in Iran.

“It’s definitely notable,” said one national Republican operative, who added that other House Republicans facing uphill reelection bids voted with Democrats on the matter.

However, the operative pushed back on the notion that it is a sign vulnerable Republicans are running away from the administration.

Last month, Michigan Rep. Tom Barrett (R) voted in favor of a war powers resolution that would have limited Trump’s authority to continue the Iran war but appeared on stage with him at a rally in Michigan days later.

“I wouldn’t read into the war powers resolution as a way of ‘oh my god, our candidates are distancing themselves from Trump’ or anything. It’s more about this issue specifically,” the national Republican operative said, noting that Barrett, Miller-Meeks and Nunn are military veterans.

Nunn has also shown he is willing to appear with administration officials in his district, including Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“The reason you send Vance to Iowa or any administration official to any battleground is you want to fire up the base, and you want to turn out the base voters,” said the GOP operative familiar with Iowa.

articles.title: Trump ally Stephen Miller leads sweeping push to accelerate removal of migrant children
articles.summary: Exclusive: key White House loyalist orchestrating multi-agency effort condemned by critics as cruel and racist
articles.body:
Stephen Miller is leading an unprecedented and intense White House drive across a host of government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist and, in some cases, flout federal law, the Guardian has learned.

As deputy chief of staff at the White House, focused on immigration policy, Miller is seen as the mastermind and enforcer behind Donald Trump's hardline anti-immigration agenda.

He is directing a whole-of-government approach that has been ramping up throughout Trump's second term and is targeting a vulnerable population of undocumented children. Many abruptly find themselves denied access to legal immigration pathways in the US, with their applications fast-tracked and then rejected before being forced out of the country.

Almost 200,000 children have been ordered removed from the US by immigration judges since Trump returned to the White House, a doubling of such court orders since January 2025, according to analysis of data from the Department of Justice's executive office for immigration review (EOIR) conducted by the California-based advocacy Mobile Pathways and shared with the Guardian. The advocacy group has focused its numbers on children appearing in immigration court, regardless of whether they arrived in the US alone or with family, and believes the total to be an undercount.

Miller has harnessed personnel and power for his task from at least five cabinet-level government departments, as described to the Guardian by several sources briefed on various initiatives, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation. The departments include Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the care of migrant children who are in the country without a parent or guardian; the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), where Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) are based; and the Department of Justice (DoJ), which houses the immigration courts – with the state department and the Department of Defense playing more subsidiary roles.

Miller frequently confers with subordinates, daily at times, pressing them to maximize removals of immigrant children from the US, according to a number of sources familiar with the White House plans.

"The folks that have to do the implementation are told, 'These instructions came directly from the White House,' or 'These instructions came directly from Stephen Miller,' as a way of conveying, you know, the importance of implementing them in a timely fashion and doing it in the way that they were instructed to do it," one source said.

Sources warned of the White House pushing each department to boost efforts individually and by working together in new ways to speed up and expand the deportation of undocumented children – especially by dismantling inter-agency communication safeguards designed to protect children, and hurrying them in vast numbers, without lawyers, in front of asylum officers and immigration judges who are either inclined or are under pressure to take a hard line and get them out of the US.

All departments involved, and the White House, were sent questions and asked for comment.

The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort to speed up the removal of undocumented children but claimed the effort was not new.

However, the White House and some other agencies that responded framed their endeavors as an anti-trafficking initiative instead of a means to enforcement.

"The Department of Homeland Security, the US Department of Health and Human Services, and the Homeland Security Council are working to locate and rescue these children. We are ensuring these children are reunited with their parents and families in their home countries," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The Homeland Security Council is a body which, under Trump, now answers directly to him within the executive office of the president of the United States and is led by Miller.

But there is no certainty that deported young people end up reunited with family and safe in their home countries, as many of them left in the first place because of threats to their wellbeing, including from their own family, or in order to reunite with parents in the US.

One source said: "This administration has shown time and again that it has no plan for children other than to disrupt their lives and endanger them … they have no credibility to claim that they are acting with children's safety as their priority."

Claire Trickler-McNulty, an immigration policy fellow at Hyphen, a nonprofit intermediary focused on racial equity, said: "A facade of trafficking is sort of a convenient, feel-good cover that has nothing to do with trafficking and everything to do with reducing the program [of federal care for undocumented children], getting rid of services, getting rid of things they don't like, and then removing kids." Trickler-McNulty was previously an assistant director at ICE and a senior counselor at USCIS during the Biden administration.

Another source said of the Trump administration: "They are weaponizing that narrative [trafficking] because it makes them out to be the good guys, and everything else makes it really clear that they're not."

Critics point out that while there are some genuine instances of exploitation within the US that were exposed during the Biden administration, including by the New York Times , the Trump administration and other rightwing politicians and commentators are using extreme, and relatively rare, examples to justify their drastic intervention.

The sweeping inter-agency effort has also left more than 1,800 undocumented immigrant children stuck in the custody of federal health officials after often having previously experienced abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harm in their countries of origin or on the way to the US. Sources believe many of those officials are collaborating with immigration enforcers while sharing children's confidential files in an unparalleled and legally dubious dismantling of bureaucratic safety firewalls.

One consequence of this strand of the anti-immigration crackdown is the sharp acceleration in the DoJ's immigration court orders to remove children from the US issued under the second Trump administration. This includes a rapid increase over this spring and summer. Removal orders rose from 7,366 a month in January 2025 to 16,200 in June, 16,750 in July and 14,744 in August, according to Mobile Pathways' research.

Of the more than 200,000 children in total that have been ordered removed under the second Trump administration, 70% were under the age of 13. The percentage of hearings ending in a removal order also more than doubled over the 20 months.

"What is my biggest fear? A lot of it is [already] happening," Trickler-McNulty said.

She is concerned by the administration gutting legal services and due process for children , closing down higher quality facilities, and having ICE officials take on senior roles in immigrant child welfare at HHS's office of refugee resettlement (ORR).

"Stephen Miller is incredibly involved in the whole immigration side, he has his daily calls, he reaches down into the agencies," she said.

Many unaccompanied children are facing the prospect of a forced return to dangerous situations in their countries of origin, particularly in Central America, including Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, or even places as unstable as Afghanistan . Many have relatives in the US whom they could live with, who are vetted by the government and are known as sponsors. But the second Trump administration has severely restricted this from happening, either through new bureaucratic methods that keep children in custody until they can be deported, or by making prospective sponsors too scared of ICE to come forward.

Adults and families embroiled in the immigration system are subject to potential detention by DHS, while unaccompanied children are supposed to be quickly transferred from that department's agencies into the custody of ORR.

This divide is by congressional design, in recognition that children in the country alone should not rely for care on the same agency that is trying to deport them, experts said.

Yet as in other policy areas, this White House is prepared to break norms.

"The Trump administration has sacrificed every element of ORR's child welfare mission on the altar of higher deportation numbers," US senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, told the Guardian. "Instead of protecting kids from human trafficking or helping them reunite with family, Trump and officials at HHS and DHS are violating children's rights [and] flouting federal law to hit quotas and satisfy their ideological crusade against immigrants. The result is significant harm and trauma to innocent children."

ORR is responsible for providing the children with a safe place to live while ensuring they have access to legal information and thoroughly vetting their potential sponsors, usually family members, who apply for their release – serving a child welfare role that has historically been separate and apart from the nation's immigration enforcement arm.

Yet "there was a rollback of that really important firewall, and there was a lot more information sharing" that kicked off in Trump's second term, one source told the Guardian.

"It's clear from who leadership is and Miller's influence and the power dynamics of this administration that, you know, if DHS wants access to a child, they're going to get access to a child," another source said. "If ICE wants access to literally every single child's identifiable information, mental health records, behavioral records, all of that, they have it. I mean, it's not about sharing at this point. They just have access to it."

Half a dozen experts and government staff have detailed, as one put it, "an unprecedented level of collaboration between agencies like USCIS, ORR and ICE and the immigration courts".

Two sources described being briefed on the White House putting together a group of officials, known as "a tiger team" in government parlance, to coordinate policy around unaccompanied children, involving DHS, ORR, the DoJ and the state department.

The result is "coercive measure after coercive measure in trying to get kids to relinquish their rights". Experts interviewed for this article describe many measures and the extent to which they required inter-agency collaboration which have not been previously reported, including:

An influx of immigration and criminal enforcement officials joining ORR in key roles, with the likely effect of shifting the agency's priorities further away from child welfare and toward mass deportations, given the expertise and point of view of its new leadership and their known closeness with Miller.

ORR having ICE officers present – and sometimes waiting to detain people – at new in-person appointments that are now part of the sponsorship process, and the two agencies appearing to share information so that prospective sponsors are detained just before or shortly after a child is set to be released from federal custody, which critics believe is not a coincidence.

ORR seemingly collaborating with USCIS to schedule and rush through asylum adjudications for the children in their custody, sometimes through unorthodox, virtual interviews, not giving the children enough time to truly prepare or consult with attorneys.

ORR receiving feedback from the White House that its policy ideas were not sufficiently punitive and Miller forcing the agency to implement new tactics with the express purpose of increasing deportations among children and their family members.

Immigration judges allegedly being told by supervisors to rubber-stamp some of the requests by ICE's attorneys who are arguing to deport immigrants – including these children – in court, with the White House watching closely.

State department officials warning some countries of origin to expect increases in deported minors.

The Pentagon being asked by HHS to supply forensic auditors to scour for fraud among legal services organizations representing the children.

In a particularly dramatic case that a source suspects of involving inter-agency collusion, enforcement agents located and detained a small child's parent just one day before the child was going to be released from ORR custody and reunited with the parent.

Then, the source said, USCIS quickly asked the child's attorneys if they wanted to withdraw their client's asylum application – given that the child no longer had a relative available to care for them.

If it was, indeed, a tactic, it was successful: that family agreed to be deported so they could finally be together and free again.

Sources said that federal rules prohibit ORR from sharing children's welfare files with ICE and this wall had typically been effective but now was being routinely disregarded.

"They're taking norms that no-one ever thought needed to be legislated … because there was at least a general understanding of how harmful it would be if they were undone. And this administration just doesn't care about harm, right? The cruelty is the intent of this," a source said.

A state department spokesperson said: "The United States expects every country to accept the return of its nationals expeditiously. The state department leads diplomatic efforts to ensure compliance with this basic responsibility."

These practices are being implemented in tandem with other policies that are keeping children in foster homes, shelters or even secure lockups, away from family, for very long periods, where many lose hope and choose to self-deport. Hundreds of undocumented children are currently being sent to Texas , where it is easier to deport them.

Federal officials have also defunded over 20,000 unaccompanied children's attorneys from nearly a hundred legal services organizations across the country, while approaching firms and anti-trafficking organizations with little immigration law experience but with ties to the administration or ICE to replace them.

Meanwhile, in a message shared with the Guardian, a Department of Defense (DoD) personnel manager sent out a recruiting request saying that the health department was urgently looking for lawyers to represent the children, seemingly from within DoD itself, which manages the nation's military. The message encouraged recipients to pursue an encore career in government and continue serving their country, touting an expedited hiring process, a $10,000 signing bonus and a competitive benefits package.

The message is unusual because it indicated the involvement of the Pentagon in child welfare and immigration matters, and because of its apparent attempt to recruit military personnel who may have only the most rudimentary understanding of immigration law and little training in trauma-informed legal representation.

"HHS considered recruiting and detailing military lawyers for temporary augmentation of capacity but is no longer pursuing this option," an unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement.

The Department of Defense referred questions to the White House and HHS.

"The erosion of due process , the dramatic attacks on both immigration courts and legal service providers , all of these feel like they are tools that are part of this larger project of essentially deporting these children by any means necessary," said Azadeh Erfani, director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC).

For some experts, Miller's widely recognized leadership of the inter-agency effort is itself concerning because of his engagement with white nationalist ideology. Miller's rhetoric frequently echoes the "great replacement theory", a racist notion that nonwhite immigrants will overrun western civilization.

For his part, Trump has said that immigrants in the US from around the world are "poisoning the blood of our country" – a line that drew comparisons to Nazism.

"There is little doubt that Stephen Miller's influence on these anti-children policies comes with racial bias," said Erfani.

Another source added: "There's some real animus towards the kids coming from Miller and his acolytes. And I think that it's also very connected to the same reason that he wants to get rid of birthright citizenship. It's about demographics, right? And he sees the kids as, like, the future generation that will, you know, continue a multiracial, multicultural vision of this country."

Miller's departmental subordinates include a number of immigration enforcement veterans who have switched from ICE to immigrant child welfare in the health department, including Angie Salazar, now the acting director of ORR, John Fabbricatore , now a senior advisor at HHS, and Dawnisha Helland, the assistant principal deputy director of the unaccompanied alien children bureau at ORR.

Their roles at HHS give ICE a potential communication channel on issues involving unaccompanied children. "All these folks used to work together," one source said.

The Trump administration repeatedly argues that its custody and enforcement policies for unaccompanied children protect them from trafficking and being taken in by relatives who pose as safe and loving while preying on or exploiting them.

"ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process. ORR is, however, involved in an inter-agency effort to locate children that arrived at the border alone during the Biden administration, and who were then release[d] to poorly vetted sponsors. In some cases, these sponsors exploited the unaccompanied children in their care, including through trafficking," the unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian.

DHS echoed that sentiment, saying that its officials were dedicated to locating children "who came across the border unaccompanied [and] were placed with unvetted sponsors who were actually smugglers and sex traffickers".

But critics reiterated their argument that this perspective is exaggerated to the point of being disingenuous.

At the same time, the administration has implemented changes to reporting child trafficking concerns that could make it harder for survivors to win asylum and other immigration relief, the Associated Press reported .

Meanwhile, one expert told the Guardian that they did not know how officials at ORR could ever again reassure a prospective sponsor that it was safe to apply for a child's release, or tell a child that they were protected, with this administration's track record.

That expert fears that families across the globe whose children are fleeing gang conscription, violence and persecution will no longer look to the US for survival. They will be too afraid of the chances of a child being swiftly detained and deported even in the typical case where the child aims to join other family members living and working in the US.

"If you're that family and you have no option for your child to be safe except sending them to the United States, now that is off the table," the source said. "And so what happens to those kids?"

Will Craft and Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting and graphics

articles.title: Lingering feuds threaten Democrats' bid to reclaim US Congress
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Democrats are seeking to reclaim Congress, but lingering divisions from a bruising run-up to the November election threaten t...
articles.body:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon holds her campaign kickoff in Orlando

WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Democrats are seeking to reclaim Congress, but lingering divisions from a bruising run-up to the November election threaten to imperil the party's attempt to claw back power from President Donald Trump's Republicans.

With control of both chambers at stake, Democrats have sought to move past the bad blood of the primaries, but in several competitive states, influential party figures have withheld endorsements or so far declined to campaign with nominees for the November 3 US midterm elections.

In ‌Maine, the governor has yet to endorse the Democratic US Senate candidate. In Texas, a congresswoman has declined to campaign alongside the state representative who defeated her in the Democratic Senate primary. In Michigan, establishment centrists are steering clear of the party's progressive Senate ‌pick. In New York, victorious democratic socialists are criticizing congressional Democrats for joining Republicans in condemning socialism. In Florida, the party has yet to rally behind its Senate nominee.

"Whether you are a progressive or an establishment Democrat or a conservative Democrat, we all have a vested interest in getting every single person over the finish line in November," said US Representative ​Summer Lee, a progressive Pennsylvania Democrat up for reelection.

If Democrats fail to unify and win at least one chamber, she warned, "all of our work after that is going to be harder."

Democrats' best path to a Senate majority requires defeating Susan Collins in Maine. Collins is widely considered the most vulnerable Republican senator in the country. But former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, is running without the endorsement of Governor Janet Mills, a onetime Senate candidate who hoped to unseat Collins herself. Mills' office did not respond to a request for comment.

"I would say they're mostly unified," Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, said of Maine Democrats. "The one piece of it that stands out is that Janet Mills has not endorsed Troy Jackson."

Contacted by Reuters, the Maine Democratic Party did not directly address Mills' role but cited turnout for its nominating process and energy on the ground as evidence of unity. "Maine Democrats ‌are united and focused on winning in November," said Devon Murphy-Anderson, the state party's executive director. "Troy has ⁠spent his career fighting for working Mainers and there is real energy behind his campaign to defeat Susan Collins."

In Texas, US Representative Jasmine Crockett has pledged her support to state Representative James Talarico, who defeated her in the Senate primary and is taking on Republican Ken Paxton. But Crockett has repeatedly rejected Talarico's overtures for the two to campaign together, even declining to introduce him at Texas Democrats' state convention in June.

Crockett drew criticism from ⁠social media users last week for appearing on stage in Texas with R&B singer Chris Brown, but not with Talarico, who could become the first Democrat in decades to win a statewide race in Texas. In 2009, Brown pleaded guilty to assaulting then-girlfriend Rihanna and has said domestic violence classes helped him learn from his mistakes.

Crockett has instead said she will focus on lower-profile races, arguing that will also benefit Talarico's Senate campaign.

"As the Democratic nominee, I trust that he has a plan," Crockett told CBS News this month. "I know that their plan wasn't necessarily to include his opponent."

In Michigan, lingering divisions have centered on Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, ​a ​progressive who narrowly leads Republican Mike Rogers in polling in one of the party's must-win states. Some Democrats have expressed discomfort with El-Sayed's association with controversial streamer Hasan ​Piker and with his rhetoric on Israel and Jews, and multiple prominent party figures have yet to endorse him.

After ‌their closely contested Senate primary, US Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan offered her "full support" to El-Sayed, and the two hugged at a unity breakfast the following day. An El-Sayed campaign adviser told Reuters the two camps are in regular communication and that the campaign sees Stevens "as a critical member of the coalition that will beat Mike Rogers."

But it's unclear whether Stevens will campaign with El-Sayed, and others in the party have been openly critical.

US Representative Hillary Scholten and state Senator Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for a congressional seat, have not endorsed El-Sayed. Neither of their campaigns immediately responded to a request for comment.

Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution – a group that works to elect progressive candidates – said there's a double-standard when progressives win against establishment candidates.

"The establishment expects progressives to fall in line when they prevail at the ballot box, but when progressives win, there are some signs of unity, but the entire establishment doesn't really fall in lockstep behind our candidates," he said. "I think that hurts our ability to do job No. 1, which is to beat the Republicans in November."

"When you run a campaign that completely shits on the establishment and then you win that campaign ... ‌then you turn around and say, 'I need this machine in order to win,' it is a little bit disingenuous," Democratic consultant Rodell Mollineau said.

TARGETING DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS 'LIKE ME'

The divisions surfaced ​on Capitol Hill earlier this month when eight moderate Democrats joined Republicans in approving a resolution condemning socialism, drawing criticism from New York democratic socialists Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire ​Valdez, who are poised to win US House seats in November after defeating establishment-backed rivals in their primaries.

"This resolution was aimed squarely at ​democratic socialists like me," Chevalier said in a statement. "We don't need a tent that shrinks from its own history. We need a unified party that takes on corporate power, gets money out of politics and delivers for working people."

In Florida, Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, defeated the better-funded retired Lieutenant Colonel Alex ​Vindman by a double-digit margin in August.

Vindman said he would stand beside her "in ​the fight against" Republican Senator Ashley Moody and has donated $825,000 to help Democratic candidates, including $400,000 to the state party to support Nixon and other Florida Democrats.

But it's less clear whether the party is as supportive of Nixon as Vindman has been.

Derrick Scott, chair of Florida's Escambia County Democratic Party, said the party's "vote blue no matter who" message, shorthand for supporting Democratic candidates, appears to come with an exception now that Nixon is the nominee.

"We still have yet to see Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic Party, come out and unequivocally and ​full-throatedly support Angie Nixon," he said.

A Democratic Party spokesperson said it's inaccurate to say the party hasn't rallied ‌behind Nixon, noting Fried recently joined Nixon and another statewide candidate for a joint press conference. The spokesperson said the party is working closely with Nixon and is frequently in touch with her team.

Chanae Jackson, the Nixon campaign's former organizing director, said ​voters are frustrated with party leaders who underestimated Nixon and Democratic organizations too often seek Black voter turnout without building durable support for Black-led campaigns.

"They want our labor, but they don't want our leadership," she said. "They want us to work like a ​dog while they take credit for it."

(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Additional reporting by Bianca Flowers; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Andy Sullivan and Howard Goller)

articles.title: Who is Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO pushing independent AI oversight?
articles.summary: Dario Amodei's plan for "embedded evaluators" to supervise AI companies gains new urgency after OpenAI's ChatGPT agents reportedly went rogue.
articles.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei believes artificial intelligence (AI) companies need the help of independent outside watchdogs to safeguard their developing technologies. But one of the organizations he believes could do the job, METR, is closely connected to the same AI safety community that has ties to Anthropic's start. Many of its leading figures have ties to a movement called "effective altruism (EA)" — the belief that evidence and careful reasoning can help maximize the good that companies and people can do with their time and resources. METR describes itself as an AI safety testing laboratory. ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS' "METR evaluates frontier AI models to help companies and wider society understand AI capabilities and what risks they pose," its website reads. Although its website and public materials don’t make mention of effective altruism, its founders have used it as a framing for their work. Beth Barnes, METR’s founder and CEO, worked at OpenAI alongside Amodei as the company developed early versions of ChatGPT. At an Effective Altruism Global event, she laid out her vision for how to maintain AI safety. "Our overall plan is — it sort of seems like it would be good if it was someone’s job to look at models and decide if they’re going to kill us, think through the ways that that might happen, anticipate them, figure out what the early warnings would be, that sort of thing," Barnes said. Similarly, Paul Christiano, who led the research around OpenAI’s efforts to ensure its models followed acceptable strategies for delivering requested results, later founded the first iteration of METR. He too has framed parts of his approach to AI safety as a form of effective altruism. "My suspicion is that it is more important for the ‘effective altruism’ movement to have a fundamentally good product and to generally have our act together than for it to grow more rapidly," Christiano said in a 2014 article. Figures like Barnes and Christiano provide informal links to Anthropic — a company that received funding from effective altruism’s largest supporters when it emerged as a way of thinking among tech moguls. Barnes and Christiano also both worked on evaluations involving Anthropic models, providing safety checks for Anthropic's flagship AI, Claude. Most notably, Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, led Anthropic's 2022 Series B financing round before his company collapsed and he was convicted in a multibillion-dollar fraud case. Before FTX's downfall, Bankman-Fried was one of the highest-profile proponents of the Effective Altruism movement, publicly saying it shaped his approach to earning and giving money. ANTHROPIC'S MORAL COMPASS ARCHITECT SUGGESTED AI OVERCORRECTION COULD ADDRESS HISTORICAL INJUSTICES RUTHLESS EXCLUSIVE: PENTAGON CTO REVEALS REASONING FOR ANTHROPIC REMOVAL Similarly, Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn led Anthropic's 2021 Series A financing round. Tallinn has been one of the Effective Altruism movement's most prominent supporters, speaking at Effective Altruism Global conferences, helping found the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute, and donating more than $1 million to the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, an organization focused on AI safety and alignment research. Amodei isn’t calling for the rest of the industry's leaders to submit to the thinking of METR, specifically. But in a recent letter, he used them as an example of the guidance he believes the industry needs. Amodei proposed a plan: accountability could come through "embedded evaluators" that would supervise AI development companies. "Each frontier AI company commits to giving ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR) whose role it is to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments, report incidents and help assess the alignment of not just completed AI models but training pipelines and processes. "Regardless of what commitments we make, the public deserves to know what is going on. We are still the ones choosing what to include and omit. Embedded evaluators will change this dynamic," Amodei wrote. Few figures in the AI space are as well known for their efforts on AI safety as Amodei. Amodei originally studied biophysics, earning a Ph.D. from Princeton in 2011. He would go on to become a postdoctoral scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine. After his studies, Amodei worked for a series of technology companies like Baidu, Google Brain, and, in 2016, OpenAI — the company that developed ChatGPT .During his time at Baidu, Amodei worked to develop speech recognition through machine learning, a kind of pattern identification. And at Google, he began working on safety while helping develop the company’s neural-net research, computer models that loosely mimics brain function. At OpenAI, Amodei continued those themes, eventually becoming vice president of research as the company developed its ChatGPT 2 and ChatGPT 3 models. In its early stages, the GPTs were asked to fill in blanks to sentences like: "Today, I went to the ______ and bought some milk and eggs," and "I knew it was going to rain, but I forgot to take my ______." But just as the company began to discover that it could amplify the power of its models through larger and larger language models, Amodei left OpenAI in 2020. He believed the company wasn’t doing enough to install guardrails on what he saw as a budding reality of the technology he had long theorized about. He also didn’t know if he could trust the company to set aside its financial interests. "When you feel that you can't trust someone, when you feel that their values are not what they say they are, when you feel that they're not honest, when you feel that they're not in it for the reasons that they say, when you see disturbing patterns of behavior, dishonesty, that makes it very hard to continue to work with a company, to continue to trust the company," Amodei said in an interview with Bloomberg earlier this year. Since leaving OpenAI, Amodei helped start Anthropic, a company that has made AI safety a key part of its makeup. Anthropic even has a sort of constitution for its flagship AI; a guiding document laying out boundaries for its research."Anthropic wants Claude to be genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive," the company wrote. BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS That directive has caused the company to clash with the U.S. Department of Defense over developing tools that could be used to autonomously target humans on the battlefield. It also refused to do work that, in its estimation, amounted to mass surveillance. Although that tension cost Anthropic a $200 million contract, Amodei believes it's time for the industry to take similar stances, especially as some companies began to report trouble controlling their own agents. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Amodei continues to believe that AI capabilities can grow safely, but only if the industry sets standards for how it achieves "safe." "I continue to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life. My desire to achieve these benefits is undimmed. But the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and — so long as we use the time we gain well — it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right," Amodei wrote in his letter.

articles.title: This swing state Republican keeps distancing himself from Trump. It may not save him in the midterms
articles.summary: Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump, turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach t...
articles.body:
YARDLEY, Pa. (AP) — Mary Ryan may be a registered Republican but she has never voted for President Donald Trump , turned off by his crass style of politics and chaotic approach to governing.

But the 60-year-old medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs has consistently backed her party's congressman, five-term Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

This year, Ryan is so fed up with Trump and his grip on Congress that she is planning to vote in November for Fitzpatrick's Democratic opponent in the 1st Congressional District, Bob Harvie, a twice countywide elected commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.

Even though Fitzpatrick has pitched himself as a voice of reason in Washington, Ryan said that "I don't see it happening."

Defections like this one could sink Fitzpatrick's reelection chances and cost Republicans their narrow U.S. House majority. As one of the few Republicans representing a congressional district won by Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential race two years ago, Fitzpatrick has done as much as any House Republican to distance himself from Trump: Fitzpatrick voted against Trump's tariffs, his signature tax legislation and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval. The lawmaker even skipped Trump's recent midterm convention in Dallas.

But that may not be enough to overcome the collateral damage of the president's sagging approval rating and soaring fuel prices because of the war.

Fitzpatrick, speaking briefly after a Sept. 11 memorial in his district, said he understands this year's political challenges and always considers what is best for his constituents with every vote.

"That's the job," he said. Representatives for Fitzpatrick did not respond to requests for a more complete interview.

Democrats have tried for years to defeat Fitzpatrick

Harvie describes the race and his decision to run in almost existential terms.

"The lack of trust in our government, the lack of trust in each other and seeing each other as enemies based just on, you know, the color of your skin, the religion you practice, who you voted for," he said in an interview this summer. "I worry about just the basic foundations of this nation."

Fitzpatrick has consistently survived challenges in his politically mixed district. He won by 13 percentage points in 2024 when Harris won by less than a single point in the district. In 2022, he won by about 10 points when Democrats were elected to the U.S. Senate and governorship. In 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden won the district by about 5 points while Fitzpatrick carried it by about 13 points.

"Every two years Democrats in Washington label Congressman Fitzpatrick as vulnerable. Every two years he wins anyway," said Robert Speel, an associate professor of political science at the Penn State campus in Erie. "It's, to some extent, possibly like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football and failing each time."

Harvie pointed to his deep roots in the district as a basis for why he could be different from previous Democrats who ran against Fitzpatrick.

"I'm not somebody who needs to be reintroduced or introduced to people of this district. And that's very, very different than any race he's ever run before," he said.

Jean Dolan, 61, is a Democratic voter from Newtown who has never backed Fitzpatrick and does not plan to this year. She has been frustrated with Trump's immigration crackdown and she worries about how anti-vaccine sentiment in his administration could affect public health. As she sees it, Fitzpatrick is not independent enough from his party's leaders.

"He's a nice guy. I know people like him a lot in the community," she said. But, she added, "you have to serve everyone in your district."

Fitzpatrick has been willing to criticize Trump

Fitzpatrick graduated with an MBA and a law degree and worked as a special agent for the FBI and as an assistant U.S. attorney. He also worked in private practice as a lawyer and accountant before running for the seat previously held by his brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, who died of cancer in 2020.

Jim Rachau, a 45-year-old photographer from Doylestown, is a registered independent who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick again this year. Rachau is not thrilled with the war or the economy, but said Fitzpatrick has earned his support with his prior public service as an FBI agent.

"You would think serving for the public good, he would have their best interest at heart," Rachau said.

In Congress, Fitzpatrick has not shied away from disagreeing with Trump. He criticized the president, for example, in April when Trump called Pope Leo XIV "weak," and captive to the "Radical Left."

"There's so many angry voices out there. We all know that's the case," Fitzpatrick said in an episode of a podcast launched this year with U.S. Rep. Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who represents a battleground district in New York. "People are sick and tired of the noise. They're sick and tired of elected officials not being focused on the kitchen table issues that people really care about."

Fitzpatrick also posts online regularly about meeting with groups across the district. He recently showed up to a picket line with striking sheet metal workers; he dropped by a local Catholic church's parish picnic; and he stopped at a community college hosting a maternity coalition.

Fitzpatrick spends millions on attack ads against Harvie

Fitzpatrick has also unleashed a wave of spending in the race already, disbursing nearly $5 million , according to Federal Election Commission records.

Negative attack ads against Harvie have mushroomed. Many claim Harvie is under FBI investigation, which the Democrat denies. He has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running some of the ads.

According to the suit, local media reported in 2020 with few details that the FBI was investigating local government and that Harvie was called to testify as a witness in the case. His attorneys say he has never been charged.

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.

No debate has been scheduled between Fitzpatrick and Harvie, but the men appeared at the same Sept. 11 memorial, standing on opposite sides of the speaker's lectern. They did not appear to speak to each other.

Ryan, the medical writer from the Philadelphia suburbs, said she is thinking less about Fitzpatrick and more about how Republicans in Congress and their reluctance to buck the president.

"Incumbents just feel they can't cross that line. If they do, they're not going to get reelected," she said. But she acknowledged that may not matter in the end. "They might not get reelected anyway."

articles.title: Healthy food is the missing piece in health savings and flexible spending accounts
articles.summary: Fruits and vegetables are the ultimate over-the-counter medicine — good for you, proven to help and something we should make easier for people to afford.
articles.body:
Our country is facing a chronic disease epidemic. Sixty percent of American adults have at least one chronic disease and we spend $5.3 trillion a year on healthcare.

In a political climate where it’s hard to agree on anything, the positive in this case is that there has been a decades-long, widespread alignment that diet and exercise are critical to reversing this trend. As CEO of an organic food provider, I am glad to see things are changing in the right direction.

So why haven’t we made more progress? As it relates to the food side of the equation, the release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s updated dietary guidelines has received a lot of attention, but every version of those guidelines for decades has lifted up the benefit of whole fruits and vegetables and for good reason.

PLOS Medicine found in a 2019 study that if Americans met their daily fruit and vegetable guidelines, they could prevent 1.93 million cardiovascular events and save $40 billion in U.S. healthcare costs. An apple a day really could keep the emergency room away. Yet only 10 percent of Americans eat the recommended amount of vegetables and only 12 percent eat the recommended amount of fruit.

This is not a consumer education problem. It’s an access problem. Tightening budgets and rising food costs shift hungry consumers to cheaper and more heavily processed foods.

On the exercise front, in June, Harvard released a new study that found that long-term resistance training increased your chances of living longer, in fact it represented a 13 percent lower risk of all-cause mortality, 19 percent lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 27 percent lower risk of neurological disease mortality.

The percentages are startling, but we’ve known about the link between exercise for so long that our federal government has gone beyond simply encouraging us to go for a run. There’s a reason the IRS allows health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts to pay for exercise apps, gym memberships and equipment.

So why haven’t we made the same possible for healthy food?

Americans have $160 billion sitting in health savings and flexible spending accounts — pre-tax money specifically earmarked for their health. Under IRS rules, they can spend it on exercise programs, prescription drugs, medical devices, acupuncture and even sunscreen.

But not on an apple. Not on a bag of spinach. Not on the organic blueberries that decades of research show can reduce the risk of heart disease, type two diabetes and certain cancers. On the contrary, a flexible spending account will allow an American family to pay for a type two diabetes drug, Metformin , but it won’t pay for the vegetables that could help someone avoid needing it.

This isn’t just ironic — it’s backwards.

More than half of American adults — 119 million people — have high blood pressure and have to take blood pressure meds they pay for with their health savings accounts. But those same accounts won’t pay for the foods proven to lower blood pressure without drugs.

We have over $160 billion in health savings account assets and roughly $30 billion in annual flexible spending account contributions, but the IRS definition of health excludes the single most evidence-backed intervention for chronic disease prevention: eating more fruits and vegetables.

Congress should expand health savings and flexible spending account eligibility to include fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables. Whole produce; not processed food disguised as health food. It takes pre-tax money that workers already earned and already saved for and lets them use it for the foods that prevent disease.

Congress should amend health savings and flexible spending eligibility to include fruits and vegetables, to allow families to use $500-$1,000 a year of that money to buy healthy fresh food. And on the executive branch side, the Make America Healthy Again Commission should include health savings and flexible spending produce eligibility in its policy recommendations.

Will this work? Well, we don’t have to look far to make a case. Two programs that empower families, SNAP and WIC, prove consumers will buy healthy food if they have access.

The Double Up Food Bucks program operates in more than 25 states and provides a $1 for $1 match for SNAP eligible families to buy fresh fruits and vegetables. The WIC program provides participants with a monthly allowance specifically to purchase fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables.

Guess what happened? The National Institutes of Health found that the Double Up Food Bucks program led people to spend more on fruits and vegetables, buy greater variety, and make them a bigger part of their grocery purchase.

There is even a recent precedent for this. In March 2020, Congress passed the CARES Act, expanding flexible spending account eligibility to include over-the-counter medications. I’d argue fruits and vegetables are the ultimate over-the-counter medicine — good for you, proven to help and something we should make easier for people to afford.

Turning around the chronic disease trends in this country won’t happen overnight. But we can’t afford to leave proven solutions on the table.

Ricky Silver is CEO of organic food provider Daily Harvest .

articles.body:
Less than a day after President Trump said he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House, all three outlets said their journalists have been turned away from the White House grounds.

President Trump said he was banning the outlets from the premises after accusing them of producing “purposefully negative stories.”

MS NOW wrote in a statement just after 8 a.m. Saturday that their “journalists were denied access to the White House grounds.”

“MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy,” MS NOW continued in their statement.

CNN reported just after 10 a.m. that their reporters were also denied access to White House grounds and Politico released a statement shortly before 11 a.m.

On Friday, AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google were all included in a lawsuit alleging “collusion” between the tech giants.

Plaintiffs claim that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating U.S. antitrust law.

The lawsuit points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for “industry-wide coordination” to “pace the frontier” of Ai development due to recent safeguard concerns.

President Trump is spending the day in Camp David Saturday after arriving late the night before, marking his third trip this year to the presidential retreat in Frederick County, Maryland.

The president is not slated to make any public appearances during his stay at the presidential retreat and will return to the White House on Sunday.

articles.title: Why is the Trump administration targeting foreign journalists?
articles.summary: A new policy disturbingly echoes those found in Russia, China and Iran, which use strict visa compliance rules to punish journalists and media outlets that report on their governments unfavorably.
articles.body:
For more than 40 years, a Reagan-era policy enabled foreign correspondents to stay in the U.S. lawfully as long as their job required. This summer, the Department of Homeland Security announced these journalists will face restrictive new visa requirements that could be abused to punish those critical of the Trump administration.

The new rules would cap journalists’ initial admission to no more than 240 days (less than eight months), eliminating a flexible and welcoming policy that has lasted decades across both Republican and Democratic administrations.

Although the U.S. has long been a champion of press freedom, the Trump administration has shown itself to be unabashedly antagonistic toward the media . The new policy disturbingly echoes those found in Russia, China and Iran, which use strict visa compliance rules to punish journalists and media outlets that report on their governments unfavorably.

Across the government, agencies have taken extreme actions to arrest and charge journalists ; issue subpoenas, including to journalists’ family members; shut down access to the White House and the Pentagon ; threaten broadcasters ; and sue news outlets . The most egregious acts have been tied to the immigration crackdown, including revoking visas , detaining and even deporting foreign journalists.

Taken together, this shows a pattern of hostility unlike any in modern U.S. history , one in which the federal government aims to pacify and impose its views on the free press and imperils the rights enshrined in the First Amendment.

For decades, the Reagan-era policy allowed journalists to work for multiple years, granting them the time and stability needed to build deep networks and trusted contacts, understand and report on American life, build expertise, lease a house, and enroll children in schools. With this flexible system, foreign journalists could broadcast a thorough and nuanced view of America’s story to their home audiences, in their own languages and cultural frames.

Homeland Security claims, without substantiated evidence, that the new requirements are needed for “national security and fraud prevention.” Yet, by its own admission, the department recognized “the lack of public data cited in the proposed rule regarding fraud and overstays specific” to journalists.

For journalists seeking a longer stay, Homeland Security would compel them to put in an extension application every 240 days to remain in lawful status, incurring additional costs, giving new biometric data, and possibly needing to be interviewed about the content of their reporting. Such intrusive and expansive scrutiny risks granting the government the power to target foreign journalists in connection with their reporting.

Before arriving in the U.S., foreign journalists undergo thorough security vetting and are interviewed by U.S. diplomats overseas. As such, the U.S. government holds comprehensive information about their resumes, their employers’ information and their purpose of travel.

The new rule has sent chills among the foreign press community , fearing how the government could go after journalists for their reporting and suppress access to independent information. In this new milieu, foreign journalists are likely to second-guess their editorial decisions and self-censor to avoid running afoul of Homeland Security monitors.

In August, reflecting a profound concern for the right to a free press, the Committee to Protect Journalists and other press freedom advocates called on the U.S. Congress to exercise its power of oversight and to block the rule.

Congress must ensure that the ability of the foreign press to undertake continuous reporting is not obstructed through administrative artifice, recognizing that the Department of Homeland Security also faces a processing backlog and is affected by budgeting disputes and agency shutdowns.

Thankfully, a federal judge intervened just before the regulations were set to go into effect, after unions and advocacy groups sued the government over the new rules. The judge, F. Dennis Saylor of Boston, said the amended policy was based on “exceptionally weak” rationales. “The weakness of the connection between the rule and its purported rationales,” he continues, “raises legitimate questions as to whether its real purpose is not to safeguard national security and protect our borders, but to achieve other, undisclosed, goals.”

We should recall that when the Reagan administration adopted flexible and enabling rules for foreign journalists, the United States was championing individual rights and freedoms in its global contest against the now-defunct Soviet Union, which was notorious for repressing free and independent journalism.

More than 40 years later, the Trump administration has turned its back on America’s proud commitment to liberty for all. Like Saylor, we must continue the fight for open inquiry, transparency and free expression.

Loghman Fattahi is the U.S. advocacy representative at the Committee to Protect Journalists , an independent, nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom worldwide.

articles.title: NEWT GINGRICH: Xi is coming to Washington. He should bring one unexpected guest
articles.summary: Jimmy Lai's release could reset U.S.-China relations as Xi Jinping prepares to meet Trump in Washington with a business delegation next week.
articles.body: When Chinese President Xi Jinping comes to Washington to meet with President Donald J. Trump next week, the agenda will be crowded. The two men will talk trade, artificial intelligence, investment and international competition — and ultimately the future of the world’s most important bilateral relationship. Reports indicate Xi is preparing to bring a substantial delegation of Chinese business executives with him — a sign of China’s interest in strengthening ties with America. No doubt, Xi wants President Trump to reduce tariffs on Chinese goods and ease other trade restrictions that are throttling China’s economy. WHAT XI WANTS FROM TRUMP AS BEIJING SEEKS LEVERAGE IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT But if Xi wants to amplify this signal and show that he’s genuinely interested in playing fair with the West, he should bring another man: Jimmy Lai. He is a British Catholic, newspaper publisher and longtime advocate of democracy in Hong Kong. In December 2025, a Hong Kong court convicted him of national security and sedition offenses (which were based on a ludicrous, draconian Chinese security law). On Feb. 9, he was sentenced to 20 years in prison. For a man of his age, this is effectively a life sentence. TRUMP LEAVES CHINA WITH BREAKTHROUGHS — AND UNFINISHED BUSINESS ON XI’S BIGGEST FIGHTS In addition to President Trump’s disapproval of Lai’s incarceration, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for his immediate release. Other governments, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and other G7 countries, have also called for Lai’s release. He has spent more than five years in prolonged solitary confinement amid, at times, incredibly hot summer conditions. This time does not count toward his two-decade sentence. He reportedly has a litany of health problems that require close monitoring, including diabetes, high blood pressure, heart issues and crippling fatigue. All the while, Lai has been denied independent specialist medical treatment. While Hong Kong authorities claim his prosecution was a matter of national security, it is clear Lai is merely being punished for participating in journalism and peaceful political activity that criticized the Chinese government. articles.title: Lawyer says 250-foot Trump arch disrupts historic sightlines cherished by veterans seeking burial at Arlington
articles.summary: Three Vietnam veterans are suing to block Trump's Great Triumphal Arch, saying it would destroy iconic views near Arlington National Cemetery.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C.—which he said would be the largest in the world—is being opposed by three Vietnam veterans who say the project would block views between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House, some of the most well-known views in and around the city. Veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, and Jon Gundersen—along with architectural historian Calder Loth—have been engaged in a months-long legal battle with the Trump administration over the "Great Triumphal Arch". "Our plaintiffs are three Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. All of them have a deep personal relationship with Arlington National Cemetery," Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group representing the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital. "Two of our veteran plaintiffs hope to be buried there." DEMS UNLOAD ON TRUMP’S LATEST DC UPDATE WITH ‘CHRISTIAN NATIONALIST’ BROADSIDE, LEGAL PUSH Trump has said the arch should be built near Arlington National Cemetery, which serves as the final resting place for more than 400,000 military service members. Critics of the project contend that the planned structure is disrespectful to the solemn character of the cemetery. In addition, the Trump administration acknowledged in a planning document that the project will have "adverse effects on historic properties". "Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking," the National Park Service wrote in the document. The nation's capital was designed to keep historic landmarks from being obscured by other structures, Sansone said. LINCOLN MEMORIAL'S HIDDEN 15,000-SQUARE-FOOT UNDERCROFT OPENS TO THE PUBLIC AFTER A CENTURY UNDERGROUND "One of the sort of central design features is that the capital has been laid out in a very deliberate way to create this uninterrupted view between the Lincoln Memorial on the east side of the Potomac River and Arlington House, the Robert E. Lee Memorial, on the west side in Arlington National Cemetery," he said. "So our plaintiffs… are really sort of concerned about the impact that this sort of enormous structure is going to have on that sort of historic symbolic view that each of them finds really meaningful," he added. GOLDEN EAGLES, LIONS AND A WINGED LADY LIBERTY TOP TRUMP'S PROPOSED 250-FOOT DC TRIUMPHAL ARCH DESIGNS Earlier this month, the administration announced that excavation work for the project would begin within the next two weeks. The plaintiffs have asked a federal judge to issue a temporary restraining order to keep the project from moving forward, saying it can't be built without authorization from Congress. TRUMP SIGNS ACT CLEARING THE WAY FOR MEDAL OF HONOR MONUMENT ON NATIONAL MALL The Trump administration has cited a 1925 law that originally authorized a pair of 166-foot columns in Washington, D.C., that were never built. Administration officials argue that past congressional approval grandfathers the triumphal arch project and allows them to avoid authorization from Congress. "The idea is that really it's just an institutional question of who gets to decide: Is it one person, the person sitting in the White House, or should it be a sort of democratic deliberative process to sort of figure out what these monuments should look like, where they should be situated, what they should commemorate, and the like," Sansone said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Congress's authorization to have a particular project built at a particular time subject to a specific price cap by a now-disbanded commission can't reasonably be relied on to authorize a totally different independent project that's going to cost way more money centuries into the future," he added.

articles.title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW denied White House access after Trump announces ban
articles.summary: Journalists from MS NOW, CNN and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump said on social media that he had banned the news outlets over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
articles.body: Journalists from MS NOW, CNN and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump said on social media that he had banned the news outlets over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.” “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS NOW said in a statement posted on X. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalists in our democracy,” it added. The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press. MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said her White House badge did not work when she arrived Saturday morning. “The officer asked me to hand over my badge,” she said on air. “He said that it was disabled. I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him.” An MS NOW photographer was also denied access, Gardner said, while one of the network’s producers was allowed onto the White House grounds. It was not immediately clear why their access differed. CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein was also turned away when she attempted to enter the grounds. Klein spent about a minute inside the security kiosk before emerging without her credential, which she said had been confiscated. CNN confirmed Saturday that its journalists were denied access. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hinderance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right,” the outlet said in a statement posted on X. “We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor,” the statement added. Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett was denied access to the grounds. She was inside the security kiosk briefly before exiting. Politico Playbook reported in its newsletter shortly afterward the outlet’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, sent a newsroomwide email about the denial, adding Haslett had her pass confiscated by the Secret Service. “We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Greenberger said. The White House declined to comment further Saturday, referring NBC News to Trump’s previous comments. In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump said media outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” Trump also warned “other outlets” would “follow” but did not specify which ones. “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said Friday. Politico Press, the publication’s communications team, said in a post on X Friday that Trump’s claims that Politico “received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked.” “POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the post said. Responding to a reporter in the Oval Office shortly after announcing the ban, Trump said the new policy was the result of “cumulative stories over the last few years.” He did not specify a particular news report, and a White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the president’s spoken comments. The move has drawn broad criticism. During a Friday speaking engagement at Colgate University from which NBC News obtained audio, former President Barack Obama said: “I’m trying to think what would have happened if I had said, ‘You know what? Fox News, you’re out of here.’ It’s unimaginable.” He added that if a certain pocket of the country agrees with the proposed restriction, “we have not developed the kind of understanding of what democracy requires,” saying people have to get to work to shore up that understanding. White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich described the move as a constitutional violation. “The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” Heinrich said in a statement. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” “The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MS NOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs,” she added. New York Times spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander also pushed back on the move. “The courts have twice found that the Trump administration violated the Constitution by suspending reporters’ White House press passes,” Stadtlander said. “The Times stands in support of the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president.” The ban is the latest in Trump’s ongoing efforts to punish news organizations and broadcasters for their coverage. Shortly after taking office, Trump banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to acknowledge his effort to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit, and the case is ongoing. Trump has also sued outlets including the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal claiming defamation. The suits against the Times and the Journal were dismissed but have since been refiled. The BBC has filed to get Trump’s suit against it tossed.
