articles.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico say their journalists have been denied access to the White House
articles.summary: The White House denied CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists access to its grounds Saturday, the networks announced, a day after President Trump said he was banning them from the premises after accusing them of producing “purposefully negative stories.” “Earlier this morning MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White…
articles.body:
The White House denied CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists access to its grounds Saturday, the networks announced, a day after President Trump said he was banning them from the premises after accusing them of producing “purposefully negative stories.”

“Earlier this morning MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS NOW wrote in a statement posted just after 8 a.m. Saturday . “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

At around 10 a.m., CNN also confirmed its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds — denouncing the ban as an “illegal assault” on its press freedom.

“CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism,” CNN said in its statement. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.”

Shortly after, Politico’s morning newsletter, “Politico Playbook,” shared a statement from the publication’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, confirming one of its reporters was also not allowed to enter the White House.

“A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter. Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House,” Greenberger said in a statement, which was first emailed to the newsroom.

Trump announced his decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “effective immediately” in a Friday Truth Social post, accusing the three outlets of reporting false information about him and his administration.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote, adding that additional news organizations could also be blocked.

MS NOW correspondent Akayla Gardner said her press badge had been disabled when she arrived at the White House for work Saturday morning; Gardner delivered the report live from outside the grounds.

She said she that, while she cleared initial security checkpoints, White House personnel stopped her when she attempted to scan her badge to enter.

“It did not work. There was a red beeping light,” Gardner said .

The MS NOW reporter said an officer then took the badge and told her it had been disabled. When asked why, Gardner said the officer told her the decision was “above him.”

Her White House credentials were confiscated, but a producer’s badge was still active, Gardner added.

Multiple free-speech groups and press organizations, including Fox News contributors , denounced the ban — arguing it violated these outlets’ constitutional right to press freedom.

MS NOW, CNN and Politico all pushed back after Trump announced his ban, each issuing responses condemning the restrictions.

Trump has long feuded with CNN, recently calling the network “crooked as hell” and “a very corrupt organization” in a June Oval Office conference. He also frequently criticizes one of its White House correspondents, Kaitlan Collins, who he described as a “corrupt reporter” with “hatred in her eyes” during the same meeting.

“Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right,” a CNN spokesperson said in a statement.

In Politico’s statement, Greenberger similarly cited constitutionality concerns with the ban, saying, “We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.”

Trump also accused Politico of receiving $8 million in government subsidies for its “Politico Pro subscription,” something the outlet has denied.

“The claims that POLITICO received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked,” Politico said in a statement.

articles.title: New poll signals movement in Talarico vs Paxton Texas Senate race
articles.summary: After weeks of tight polls, a new survey shows one candidate breaking away in the Texas Senate race with Election Day a month out. Here's the breakdown.
articles.body:
A new Texas Pulse poll shows the Democrat widening his lead over the Republican in the Texas Senate race , with Election Day more than a month away.

Published Sept. 17, the ReconMR/Texas Pulse poll showed that Democrat James Talarico 's lead has grown to 6 points — outside the poll's margin of error — over Republican Ken Paxton , 49%-43%.

"This movement can also be seen by looking at independent voters who now favor Talarico by 40 points, 64-24%, up from 23 points, 53-30% in July," ReconMR Senior Research Analyst Lindsey Hendren said.

Here's a deeper look at the poll and how it compares to other September polls.

James Talarico widens lead over Ken Paxton in Texas Senate race

The latest Texas Pulse poll was conducted Sept. 8 to 11 among 614 likely Texas voters and has an overall margin of error of 4.3 percentage points.

The poll found that Paxton has a negative favorability rating — 38%-55% — down slightly from 40-52% in July. Talarico has a positive favorability rating of 50-39%, up from 46-39% in July.

When asked who they think will win the election, 48% of voters say Talarico while 45% say Paxton.

The poll also found another shift: a quarter of voters didn't have an opinion about Talarico in June — now it's just 10%.

"Paxton's Senate bid is being undermined by defections from within his own party," Hendren said. "While nearly all Democrats say they are supporting Talarico, just under 9 in 10 Republicans say they are supporting Paxton."

articles.title: Beware of politicians claiming to protect us from the press
articles.summary: This week, it became apparent that everyone believes in a free press, as long as it costs them nothing. Politicians in both parties are now using their offices to insulate themselves from opposing coverage — all in the name of protecting the public or the press. President Trump has ordered the banning of critical media…
articles.body:
This week, it became apparent that everyone believes in a free press, as long as it costs them nothing.

Politicians in both parties are now using their offices to insulate themselves from opposing coverage — all in the name of protecting the public or the press.

President Trump has ordered the banning of critical media companies from the White House. Meanwhile, Democrats are fighting to block a corporate media merger on equally raw political grounds.

At the White House this week, President Trump declared, “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW … and Politico.” He then added that he did not understand why the courts allow the media to print “fake news,” raising the possible addition of censorship to banishment.

On Capitol Hill and across the country, Democrats were pursuing their own political litmus test for media. Twelve blue states are in court seeking to block the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance. While framing their claims in dubious antitrust terms, many admit that they are trying to protect one of the very companies banned by Trump as a liberal platform: CNN.

Previously, Democrats shut down the government in part over a decision to withdraw government subsidies for another liberal news outlet , National Public Radio. Years ago, some Democrats even asked cable companies to consider dropping Fox News .

Both Trump and the Democrats are oblivious to the implications of their actions, blinded by the political costs of a free press and a free market.

There is little recognition, let alone remorse, among these politicians. For Trump, many in the public rallied to his side in condemnation of media bias during the last election. I have joined in the criticism of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico for their coverage. But this ban is a frontal assault on the free press itself, shattering long-standing principles maintained by past presidents.

Presidents have long condemned the media. George Washington referred to them as those “ infamous scribblers .” Thomas Jefferson complained that “Nothing can now be believed which is seen in a newspaper. Truth itself becomes suspicious by being put into that polluted vehicle.” Yet they recognized that their oath to uphold the Constitution included a sacred duty to preserve and protect the free press.

For the Democrats, the opposition to the merger is equally transparent. Figures such as former Obama administration official Norm Eisen have opposed the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger as an attack on democracy itself. Their aim is to prevent the conservative David Ellison, chairman of Paramount Skydance, from gaining control of CNN as well as existing media assets such as CBS. Despite using antitrust law, he and others have made it plain that their aim is to preserve CNN and other outlets as liberal allies.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) declared that it is a power grab by the “oligarchs,” and that Ellison gaining control of CNN is “not acceptable. This merger must be opposed.”

Former Obama adviser Dan Pfeiffer called on Democrats to stop the merger to prevent an effort to “make CNN more MAGA-friendly.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) has warned that allowing the merger will “subvert CNN’s editorial independence.”

Notably, while MS NOW, CNN, and many of these individuals are condemning Trump’s announcement, they have eagerly joined the movement to block a lawful merger on political grounds. Others have pitched a deal where the merger can go through, but that they want CNN as “a strong consolation prize,” presumably to be sold to a liberal owner.

Again, there is little thought of the costs. There rarely is. When Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and others took credit for blocking the merger of Spirit Airlines with JetBlue, they declared it a victory for the Biden administration and the Democrats. Spirit Airlines then went bankrupt and all of its employees were fired.

In this case, CNN may be the Spirit Airlines of the media. It has been struggling with both revenues and ratings, despite occasional spikes. While the Democrats want to preserve the liberal platform that regularly features their interviews and narratives, CNN often operates dangerously to the baseline on the key advertising demographic needed to keep the lights on.

Warner Bros. has lost billions. The merger would be good for both companies and their employees. Under the guise of opposing a monopoly, Democrats are opposing a deal that has been cleared by the European Commission and once-skeptical experts.

I have worked for four networks as a legal analyst for 30 years, and I want CNN to flourish. We need strong media companies. That means that we need to support both the free press and the free market in maintaining journalistically and financially strong media companies. That often means setting aside our personal disagreements with coverage to oppose political manipulation of the media by either party.

I previously have written about the media and free speech in an “ age of rage. ” Presidents and politicians have periodically allowed their anger or interests to overwhelm their judgment. President John Adams declared, “The liberty of the press is essential to the security of the state.” Yet, his administration targeted reporters and writers under the infamous Alien and Sedition Acts.

Politicians are again using their power to manipulate the press by limiting their exposure to media criticism. They are seeking to control what the public reads and watches to protect us from “fake news” or “corporate messaging.”

For centuries, politicians have played on our anger or partisanship to target the media. To defend the free press and the free market is not to agree with these companies or their coverage. It is to defend our right to make our own decisions on what news to read and whom to believe.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution . “

articles.title: These were the hottest baby names 50 years ago. What happened?
articles.summary: There’s a good chance that, if you’re in your 50s, your name is one of three that were topping the charts in the 1970s.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – There’s a good chance that if you’re turning 50 this year, your name is Jennifer or Michael or Jason. There’s also a pretty good chance that if you are a grandparent or will be soon, the newest member of your family will not have at least two of those names.

The odds are relatively high that, instead, their name will be Liam or Olivia or one of the handful of others that have been incredibly popular in recent years .

Before Liam and Olivia became the most popular baby names in the U.S., it was Michael and Jennifer at the top of their respective lists. A Nexstar review of data from the Social Security Administration shows that in 1976, Jennifer was the most popular name for newborn girls in every state, while Michael was the most popular for boys in 34 states. Jason claimed the top spot in 15 others, while James was No. 1 in two.

The SSA reports that between 1926 and 2025, more than 1 million Jasons have been born, making it the No. 26 boy name overall across the time period. There have been more than 1.4 million Jennifers over the same span, making it the third-most-popular name for girls.

They weren’t in the limelight forever, though. It’s been at least a decade since Jason even landed in the top 100 baby names for any state, and even longer for Jennifer.

It was those Jennifers and Jasons, and likely their friends, who helped break the trend.

As Steph Coffield , a baby name advisor for BabyCenter, explains, Jason began losing popularity after “all of those Jasons became new dads.”

“At that point, names that ended in ‘-son’ started to explode in popularity — like Jackson, Mason, Bryson and others. They felt familiar since they had the same ending as ‘Jason,’ but distinct,” she explained.

Similarly, when Jennifers — or Jens or Jennies or whatever nickname they had to go by because of another Jennifer in their school or workplace — became moms, they, too, “wanted their children to have more distinctive names,” Coffield said.

There’s another aspect, too. The popularity of Jennifer in the 1970s and 1980s is an example of a name that became “tied to that generation.” Colleen Slagen , the baby name consultant behind NamingBebe.com , explained that “by the time the next generation starts having kids, Jennifer feels like a ‘mom name.’”

There are some names that, despite how popular they may become, have never faded. That includes Michael and James, which Slagen described as “founding father” type names. They haven’t ranked outside the top 100 ever. James hasn’t even fallen out of the top 20.

“These are timeless names with more stable popularity curves [versus] the steep peak we saw with Jennifer and Jason,” Slagen explained via email.

“I think that because names today are less saturated — that is, people are choosing from a wider pool and the popular names aren’t used with the same frequency that they were in past generations — we will see fewer ‘timestamped’ names,” Slagen said, noting, though, that some names may still fall into that category.

We could be on the precipice of watching some popular names become “extinct.” Earlier this year, BabyCenter predicted several boy names ending in -y — Huxley, Grady and Harry, for example — are among those that could soon fade like Jason and Jennifer. Unique spellings of normal-sounding names, like Maddison and Alivia, may also be destined for history.

Social media suggests Gen Z — some of whom are likely too young to have children — have already declared “Jessica” the newest iteration of “Karen,” potentially setting it up for extinction.

There may be a reason why names rapidly lose prevalence. Slagen told Nexstar in 2024 that she encourages people to avoid trendy names.

“Any name that jumps over 100 spots a year in popularity … in my mind, that’s the sign of a name that’s going to go out of fashion,” she explained, adding that she suggests soon-to-be parents consult the Social Security Administration’s annual rankings of the top-used baby names in the country.

If you want to know whether or not your name is extinct, you can use the Social Security Administration’s lookup tool , which can show how popular it was each year.

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
articles.summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters' White House press badges were confiscated, the outlets reported.
articles.body:
Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets .

An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported.

Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized.

Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

Press freedom advocates called the move unconstitutional.

"The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.

CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.

Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass.

All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".

MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".

Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights.

And CNN said, "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."

Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called out Trump's White House ban as illegal and unconstitutional.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.

It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.

Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

Judge swapped in Trump's defamation case against BBC

articles.title: Congressman Tom Barrett: 'Being a socialist should disqualify him for people's consideration in my district'
articles.summary: Michigan's Tom Barrett is locked in a tight race in the Lansing-based seventh district against William Lawrence, founder of the Sunrise Movement.
articles.body: Control of Congress may very well run through Michigan's seventh district. Anchored by Lansing, the state capital, it features a large blue city, surrounded by reddish suburbs, and deep red rural areas. It is consistently described as one of the closest swing districts in the country. Freshman Congressman Tom Barrett narrowly won the district in 2024, and is now locked in a tight race with William Lawrence, an activist and founder of the climate change-focused Sunrise Movement. Barrett is a 21-year Army veteran helicopter pilot, who served numerous deployments overseas, before returning to Michigan and spending nearly a decade in the state legislature. 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS The race has recently been roiled by a series of controversial social media posts. In some of them, Lawrence called the nuclear family "an isolating, violent way of organizing society" and praised campaigns to abolish the police. He now claims that his views have changed. Barrett argues that the newfound shift is about political expediency, not genuine conviction: "I think we got to take him at his word that this was his absolute true ideology and it wasn't just this one statement that he made. He made repetitive statements against police, calling to not just defund but abolish the police altogether. He wanted to throw open the borders. He said if we're a humane country, we've got to throw open the borders and redistribute all of the wealth. "He called the nuclear family a violent way to organize society, as you said. Countless other statements that he's made and other things that he has done that show a pattern of behavior that this is not an isolated incident. "And obviously it's clear to any neutral observer that he is doing this because he is running in a competitive district trying to get elected to Congress. He's not running in Rashida Tlaib's district or AOC's district where they're far more sympathetic to these DSA-aligned socialist candidates. He's running in the district that I live in where I'm raising my own nuclear family." Barrett contends that the implementation of Lawrence's border and immigration policies would pose a clear and present danger to the safety of Americans: "Well, the foremost obvious risk of these open border policies of my opponent is just starting with the public safety threat. So take out all of the other economic factors: just the physical threats to our communities are substantial. "There are criminal gang activities. We have cartels that were freely operating both ways across the border under the Biden administration. We had upwards of ten or even fifteen million illegal immigrants that came into our country completely unvetted." Barrett also argues that the fentanyl crisis is directly tied to border and immigration policies as well. "The leading cause of death of Americans my age wasn't cancer, wasn't heart disease, it was fentanyl overdose deaths. People that I served with in the military that came home and survived combat and died of fentanyl overdose…because of drugs that were pouring across our border. "For the first time in my life, we have seen a significant decline in fentanyl overdose deaths, really because of the efforts…to secure our border, and my opponent, William Lawrence, would entirely reverse that, throw the border open again, abolish the police at the same time. "And we can only assume the outcome of that would be far more Americans dying of fentanyl deaths, as well as gang activity and other tragic circumstances that arise when you have an open border and no public safety to protect Americans." William Lawrence is also a longtime member of the DSA (Democratic Socialists of America), but recently claims that he let his membership lapse. Barrett argues that Lawrence remains a fervent believer in socialist ideology, but is merely trying to downplay his true beliefs to win a competitive race: "Well, I think being a socialist should disqualify him for people's consideration in my district. You look at the tenets of socialism and what they want to do and the endorsement of that. MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC CANDIDATE TRIES TO JUSTIFY DELETED POSTS THAT REVEAL FAR-LEFT BELIEFS "My opponent…cleverly claims that he let his membership lapse, I don't know, two weeks before the primary election on the eve of him winning…to face off against me in one of the most competitive congressional races in the country that will arguably decide control of the House of Representatives. "So he doesn't disavow the democratic socialists…He has embraced all of their positions, gathered all of their support, really benefited from the support of the democratic socialist movement. "And then when the time comes to defend those positions, he wants to say, well I let my membership lapse so you can't hold me accountable for all their positions. But I didn't leave under any actual disagreement with them. I'm simply leaving for political reasons because he's so focused on trying to win this election in a desperate attempt to not be accountable to his own record, but to distract away from the devastating effects of socialism and what that would mean for our country if he were to be elected." Perhaps the most controversial of Lawrence's statements involved a post expressing frustration and outrage with politicians on climate policy. Lawrence, specifically targeting West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin, wrote: 'Hurry up and die so that we can get started." Barrett believes that this type of rhetoric should put the voters of the seventh district on high alert: "Obviously that's entirely inappropriate, something that should really raise the attention of every single reasonable American to say that that's not how we go about our rhetoric here in our country. Politics is a full contact sport…but I've never in my political life, in any campaign, called on political figures to 'F you and hurry up and die.' "And that shows the radicalization…He was a founding member of the Green New Deal Alliance in Michigan, calling to ban gasoline-powered vehicles that we build in my district that employ thousands of people in my district." Midterm elections generally hinge on economics and affordability issues are driving the political narrative today in tight races around the country. Barrett makes the case that congressional Republicans have delivered on everyday pocketbook issues: "Well, we lowered costs on people's taxes, certainly…and we expanded the child tax credit. We saved families taxes to the expanded standard deduction, streamlined filing for individuals. No taxes on tips, no taxes on overtime, no tax on Social Security. I wanna take that a step further and have no taxes health care. Give every American a tax-exempt health savings account and expand the things that they can use it for, for healthy groceries, gym memberships, fitness equipment. "Obviously bring down the cost of gas as well with the conflict in Iran that I have again voted my conscience on as well and want to see gas prices come down and that will affect a lot of other parts of the economy as well around affordability. These are things that we can face. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But if we hand our country over to radical socialists who are simply going to tax Americans to death and then pass on benefits to illegal immigrants and people who refuse to go to work and participate in the economy. We will be worse off for that. "So this is a very, very important election. I stand on my own merits. I know what I've done here in Congress. It's my job to go out and make the case to the voters in my district, and contrast that with the exact things that my opponent has said what he has stood for and what his pattern of behavior has shown in what he would do if he were elected to Congress."

articles.title: FAA says proposed Trump arch will require ‘eternal flame’ on top to alert pilots
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said Saturday that President Trump’s proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C., would require an “eternal flame” on top to alert nearby pilots. “The FAA’s determination includes conditions for the Arch to be appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said Saturday that President Trump’s proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C., would require an “eternal flame” on top to alert nearby pilots.

“The FAA’s determination includes conditions for the Arch to be appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the Arch to make it noticeable for pilots,” an FAA spokesperson told The Hill.

The agency released a hazard study Friday that confirmed the Triumphal Arch “would not pose a hazard to aircraft” after a review by safety experts that examined “airspace, air traffic patterns and procedures around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, as well as operations at nearby military/public-use airports.”

The FAA previously stated the arch would ​need red obstruction lights, such as the light at the top of the Washington Monument, but said the structure no longer is required to ​have them in its hazard report, according to the New York Times .

A letter to the National Park Service (NPS) about the study also detailed that the searchlight projectors that would accompany the “eternal flame” should “provide an average illumination of at least 15 foot-candles (161.46 lux) over the top one-third of the structure.”

The proposed Triumphal Arch would become the largest in the world, towering over the Monumento a la Revolución in Mexico City, measured at 220 feet, and the 164-foot Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

It would be located along the Arlington Memorial Bridge, which symbolically represents the reunified U.S., connecting the North and South following the Union victory that closed the Civil War in 1865.

A veterans group launched a campaign last week against the arch, arguing it was “entirely inappropriate and borders on sacrilege to the men and women buried” at the cemetery to break the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery with the arch.

A NPS assessment said in August that the arch would adversely impact dozens of historic sites around the city, including by obstructing views.

It listed nearly 40 locations across the city after the agency asked outside groups to comment, including the Pentagon, the Washington Monument, the U.S. Capitol, the National Mall Site, the Lincoln Memorial, the Robert E. Lee Memorial and Lyndon B. Johnson Memorial Grove.

articles.title: Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty
articles.summary: COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, aft...
articles.body:
Special Report: How Trump's threats to seize Greenland have upended the island's push for independence

By Stine Jacobsen, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little

COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic ‌island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached an agreement ‌for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made ​public, including the scale of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.

"Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke ‌Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook ⁠on Saturday.

"A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he ⁠said.

But some residents in Greenland's capital Nuuk expressed scepticism about closer ties with Washington.

"The US should not control Greenland. I think it's better if we have cooperation with NATO," said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65.

"Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland," Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk. "He should not expect our ​children ​and grandchildren to become Americans in the future."

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that ​Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and ‌accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on Truth Social on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively ‌reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably ​not the end of President Trump's ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of ​US strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby ​Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.

If Copenhagen cedes any formal authority to Washington, it raises ‌the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of ​replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with ​a colonial relationship to the United States," he said.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a Facebook post on Saturday that the proposed deal "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."

Trump's threats, which peaked in January, ​triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO ‌and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, ​which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Additional reporting by ​Tim Barsoe in Nuuk and Lili Bayer in Brussels; Editing by Ros Russell)

articles.title: The Memo: Trump doubles down on demand for ‘recognition’ in Kennedy Center fight
articles.summary: President Trump is doubling down on his insistence that he needs “recognition” from the Kennedy Center in return for planned renovations. Trump’s assertion Friday afternoon seems to mean he is holding fast to his demand that his name should be added to the center in some shape or form — even though a court ruled…
articles.body:
President Trump is doubling down on his insistence that he needs “recognition” from the Kennedy Center in return for planned renovations .

Trump’s assertion Friday afternoon seems to mean he is holding fast to his demand that his name should be added to the center in some shape or form — even though a court ruled against him on that score this past week.

“If we’re going to save the Kennedy Center, I think the Trump administration should be given recognition for doing so,” the president told reporters during an Oval Office encounter that was otherwise dominated by his declaration that he would ban three news organizations — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — from the White House.

The furor over the Kennedy Center has consumed much of the week, with developments coming thick and fast.

First, a judge reaffirmed that Trump’s name cannot be added to the performing arts center unless Congress were to approve such a change.

The legislation that created the Kennedy Center characterizes it as a “living memorial” to President John F. Kennedy, assassinated in Dallas in 1963. Therefore, the courts have taken the view that a decision made by Congress can only be amended by Congress — not by a vote of the Trump-friendly board of the center nor by fiat by the president himself.

Following that court decision, the board announced the center’s closure in a move ostensibly prompted by a need for repairs and by fragile finances. It’s widely accepted that some renovations are necessary, but Trump’s opponents on the issue have contended repairs could be made in stages while the center remains open.

Trump himself then raised the specter of the Kennedy Center, which officially opened in 1971, being demolished — or “ripped down,” as he put it. This in turn appears to have spurred a judge on Thursday to stipulate that 30 days’ notice would be required before any significant changes — including demolition — could be made to the building.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said he was making the ruling in part to “avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events.”

At Friday’s appearance in the Oval Office, Trump attacked Cooper as “conflicted” and “very hostile.”

He also assailed the congresswoman who has become his nemesis on the issue, Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), as “a person that never did a thing in her life, frankly — never did anything constructive. All she does is complain.”

Beatty is an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, and she has led the legal challenges to Trump’s plans — with significant success so far.

By Beatty’s account, she and Trump had a fiery argument during a virtual meeting of the board earlier this week. Beatty told Luke Russert of MS NOW’s “The Weeknight” that the president was “unhinged … hollering and screaming” during the exchange, which she said went on “for a good eight or nine minutes.”

In any event, Trump did not explicitly repeat his threat to demolish the Kennedy Center during his Oval Office remarks Friday.

Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action was co-counsel for Beatty along with the Washington Litigation Group in this week’s action.

Eisen told this column he did not expect Trump to press ahead with a demolition — a scenario that he contrasted with the ongoing work to create a new ballroom at the White House.

“I think the restriction will hold,” Eisen said. “There was no court order in place when the East Wing was destroyed. Here, we have a court order, and it’s one that has been affirmed. The Trump administration will follow court orders if you reiterate them often enough.”

Eisen also contended that Trump had behaved counterproductively for his own interests.

“He said the quiet part out loud, which was very unfortunate for his case — essentially, ‘If it can’t be named for me, I’m going to blow it up.’”

Trump has fought a long battle to have his influence embedded into to the famous arts center.

Early in his second term, he fired several board members including the chair, appointed loyalists as new board members and said he would be made chair — which he was.

The board late last year voted to amend the institution’s name to “The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” and signage was affixed reflecting the change.

A judge ruled against the change in May, and Trump’s name was removed the following month — though tarp has been erected around the lettering ever since, seemingly to conceal evidence of a presidential defeat.

The whole episode has drawn enormous media attention. The question of how much it will matter politically, especially with the midterm elections little more than six weeks away, is hotly debated.

Republicans argue that, for all the sound and fury, it’s not going to be a major issue.

“It matters a lot in D.C. to people who love the Kennedy Center, and it appears to matter a lot to bookers for CNN and [MS NOW],” said Republican strategist Matt Mackowiak. “It’s not clear to me it matters to voters. I think most people don’t know what the Kennedy Center is.”

Mackowiak did — sparingly — acknowledge that there could be some impact if the controversy fuels the idea that Trump is overly fixated on himself rather than on issues more pertinent to voters’ lives.

“The only way they would care is if the president is devoting too much time to an issue like that, which appears trivial to most Americans,” he said. “But the idea that gas prices would be lower if he didn’t take try to take over the Kennedy Center is absurd.”

Democrats, naturally, see it very differently.

“Insisting his name be imposed on a living memorial to a dead president who was assassinated is really going to upset a lot of people, including some who might otherwise support some of his policies,” said Democratic strategist Tad Devine.

Devine acknowledged the issue would not be the be-all and end-all for the election.

But he linked it to Trump’s other efforts in Washington — including the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial and a proposed arch, as well as the White House ballroom. He argued that such matters can resonate, in part because they are so different from orthodox political topics.

“He’s taking the nation’s capital and trying to turn it into his own advertising scheme,” Devine argued. “This isn’t going to drive the election, but I do think it really cuts through.”

He added: “People understand what he’s trying to do and they don’t like it.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Thousands join protest outside Kennedy Center, expressing concern that Trump might tear it down
articles.summary: Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump’s plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organizations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump’s plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organizations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution. The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in “Hands Around the Kennedy Center.” At one point some held hands and formed a human chain around the center. Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to keep Trump’s plans for the building at bay. One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites onto its governing board. Late last year, he had his named placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed. The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.” Raleigh said the Kennedy Center is more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he doesn’t believe the president fully understands why people are so upset “but that’s our job right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be.” A landmark of the performing arts has gone silent Protesters talked about the importance of the center as the pinnacle of the nation’s performing arts world. Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump’s name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts. “The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” Wilkinson said. “This is not just about putting the president’s name on the Kennedy Center. It’s about censoring the performances and the programming. That’s what started all this. So that’s what the nitty-gritty really is about this. So I want to replace all of this with love. That’s why there’s a heart.” Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts have with the center and how those relationships might be impacted by what’s going on. Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the center had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. “I mean, they borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington,” she said. They also performed on the center’s Millennium Stage. “All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart,” Baciu said. Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart- wrenching. “This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank,” she said of the throngs present. “This was my visceral response to this. I’ll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it’s going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilized people.” Friday’s event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continues pushing for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump’s triumphal arch and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the U.S. Institute of Peace. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it. “We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it,” he said. “I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognized as having saved the Kennedy Center.”

articles.title: Bill Maher hammers Macklemore over Gaza remarks, highlights rapper's controversial 'Jew' costume from 2014
articles.summary: Bill Maher revived Macklemore's 2014 prosthetic nose controversy on "Real Time" while mocking AOC's response to the Ed Sheeran tour fallout.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher doubled down on his criticism of rapper Macklemore on Friday, reviving a 12-year-old costume controversy and suggesting that "everyone is just really so stupid." During Friday’s episode of HBO’s "Real Time," Maher continued his criticism of Macklemore, 43, after the "Thrift Shop" singer was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s "Loop Tour" following a string of anti-Israel remarks. "Everyone’s paying more. Macklemore had to pay an arm and a leg for a giant fake prosthetic ‘Jew’ nose," Maher said, referring to an onstage costume worn by Macklemore in 2014 in which he wore a dark wig, beard and fake nose. Shortly after the incident, Macklemore issued an apology on his website, saying, "Family, friends and fans alike who know me well, know that I'm absolutely not the person described in certain headlines today. There is no worse feeling than being misunderstood, especially when people are hurt or offended." BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM Maher continued discussing the controversy, pointing to Macklemore’s previous comments about the Israel-Hamas war. "Apparently, [Ed Sheeran] is old buddies with Macklemore from 15 years ago, back when Macklemore had his one hit," he continued. "So, Ed Sheeran let Macklemore be his opening act on his tour. And when I say, ‘act,’ he goes out there and repeats lies about how Gaza is a genocide." MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE He added, "Not that they care, but that’s a lie." "Everyone is just really so stupid," he added. "Listen to this, AOC was asked yesterday would she change the channel on the radio if Ed Sheeran came on. And she said, ‘Yes. Yes, I would.’ You know, AOC? Way ahead of you. I’ve always changed the channel when [Ed Sheeran comes on]." MACKLEMORE BAN BY ROBERT KRAFT DRAWS FIRE FROM AOC AND CAIR WHO ADVOCATE FOR FREE SPEECH ONLY WHEN CONVENIENT The "Real Time" host then pivoted to the dispute between Macklemore and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. Macklemore said in an Instagram post that Sheeran told him Kraft would not allow the rapper to perform at Gillette Stadium, which the Kraft Group owns. "Ok, so Robert Kraft, who is a rich guy owns the Patriots, owns the stadium where this concert was about to take place, he was understandably offended by this and said, ‘You can’t play my stadium,’" Maher said. "So, now Macklemore’s fans hate Ed Sheeran. Ed Sheeran’s own band won’t play with him. And Ed Sheeran needs a new opening act." BARSTOOL CHIEF DAVE PORTNOY BLASTS MACKLEMORE'S SHADY PAST, STRONGLY SUPPORTS PATRIOTS OWNER ROBERT KRAFT Later in the show, Maher returned to his criticism of musicians using concerts to promote political causes. "But I think just any kind of echo of that old cancel culture from the past is going to be a loser in today's environment," Maher said. "Is anyone looking for any of this at a concert? I mean, do I really need a lecture on politics of any stripe right when the molly is kicking in? It's so arrogant on both their sides." MICHAEL RAPAPORT CHEERS MACKLEMORE GETTING DROPPED FROM ED SHEERAN'S TOUR, SAYS 'F--- YOU' The comments come on the heels of the highly publicized Sheeran-Macklemore story, in which Macklemore told the crowd at a New Jersey show that, "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." After being dropped from the tour, Macklemore donated $1 million dollars to Palestinian aid efforts — prompting Kraft to make a $2 million donation to Gaza after the rapper called on him to match the amount. ROBERT KRAFT PLEDGES $2M FOR HUMANITARIAN AID AS MACKLEMORE FACES FALLOUT OVER VENUE BAN Maher’s comments drew criticism from political commentator Kaivan Shroff, who told Fox News Digital the comedian’s approach of blasting musicians for sharing their political opinions has an underlying tone of hypocrisy. WATCH: Why Macklemore Got Kicked Off Ed Sheeran’s Tour "Maher’s whole premise falls apart the minute he starts mocking celebrities for having political opinions. Bill Maher is a celebrity with an opinion on virtually everything. He can think Macklemore is wrong, AOC is ridiculous or Ed Sheeran is overrated. But pretending the problem is that entertainers are weighing in on politics is absurd when that has been his own business model for decades," Shroff said. The former Hillary Clinton campaign staffer then pointed to Maher’s rehashing of Macklemore’s 2014 costume incident. "The Macklemore costume is relevant, especially given the subject matter. But Maher takes that legitimate point and buries it under a bunch of cultural sniping," Shroff told Fox News Digital. MIKE HUCKABEE CALLS OUT MACKLEMORE ON ANTISEMITISM: 'VOICE' OF 'JEW HATRED' "AOC said she would change the station because of Sheeran’s involvement in the controversy, Maher jokes that he changes it because he dislikes Sheeran’s music. That may get a laugh, but it does not actually respond to her position in any meaningful way. The same is true of calling Macklemore a one-hit wonder. None of that tells us whether the underlying argument is right or wrong." As the fallout continues, Axia Public Relations CEO Jason Mudd said Sheeran should make a decision and stick to it. "Every hour of silence gives someone else the opportunity to control the narrative," Mudd told Fox News Digital, adding, "Strong crisis decisions share three things: They're fast. They're clear. They're final. Sheeran doesn't need a new decision. He needs one decision he can stand behind." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I'll stick to Sheeran's own communication strategy here, not the politics behind it," Mudd continued. "If Sheeran were my client, I'd advise him to pick a direction and hold it. One clear explanation is enough. Circling back to it in public is a common mistake. It’s perceived as doubt and invites more discussion and debate." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Macklemore’s representatives for comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to Sheeran's representatives as well.

articles.title: Millions of new cyber-immigrants are invading America and coming for your job
articles.summary: Writer John Mac Ghlionn warns that the rise of automated systems threatens the stability of the American middle class by eroding worker bargaining power and displacing specialized professionals.
articles.body:
Right-wing commentator Joe Allen recently warned that Silicon Valley is releasing a wave of “algorithmic immigrants.” These digital workers operate around the clock from server farms, threatening millions of American jobs. They never ask for health insurance. They don’t take sick days, and they never request a raise.

You can spend all day arguing about whether software deserves to be called an “immigrant,” but that misses the point.

A mid-level white-collar employee works about 2,000 hours a year. Software deployed across a cloud cluster can run 8,760 hours a year without stopping.

The real damage comes long before anyone receives a pink slip. Employers realize that total termination is unnecessary when the mere threat of automation obliterates a worker’s bargaining power. A senior analyst walks into an annual review asking for an 8 percent cost-of-living adjustment. The executive on the other side of the desk opens a browser tab displaying a platform that handles 70 percent of that analyst’s daily output. The raise vanishes, replaced by a passive-aggressive suggestion that the employee should feel lucky to retain their job.

Gen X and millennials were taught to memorize a very specific script. Go to college and accumulate tens of thousands of dollars in debt. Learn to process structured information, then secure a spot in an air-conditioned office. The educational system spent decades producing workers tailored for a world that required human minds to summarize reports, draft contracts, write software, and analyze spreadsheets. Suddenly, machines that do those exact tasks are cheaper and faster. The rules of the economic board game changed while millions of people were still paying off the degrees they bought to play it.

Politicians and tech executives love to fall back on the classic post-industrial cheerleading routine. They tell displaced workers to retrain, pick up a new technical skill, and adapt to the modern economy. Telling a 45-year-old paralegal to learn software development sounds reasonable right up until the software itself starts writing code faster than a senior computer science graduate.

Telling workers to constantly outrun an automated system that updates itself every few weeks is a recipe for psychological and financial exhaustion. People have families, property taxes, and health insurance payments that don’t magically pause while they spend three years attempting a mid-career pivot.

A company doesn’t need to fire its entire staff to trigger an economic disaster. Reducing a hundred-person department to 60 workers creates an immediate surplus of 40 unemployed specialists competing for a dwindling pool of desks. That surplus depresses wage growth across the entire sector. Yet the company’s output grows and profits increase. The enterprise wins while more Americans can no longer live in their neighborhoods or make their mortgage payments.

The gap between how businesses perform and how everyday citizens live will become even harder to ignore. Technically, America can get economically richer and individually poorer at the same time.

The middle class bears the brunt of this transition, largely because middle-class jobs consist overwhelmingly of information management. Managing calendars, writing marketing copy, and translating internal memos form the backbone of the suburban tax base. Losing an entry-level service job certainly disrupts a young person’s plans, but losing a $100,000 professional salary could destroy a family.

Telling displaced office workers to switch to physical trades sounds great in an op-ed, but reality hits hard on the job site. A former copywriter can’t become a licensed electrician by next Wednesday morning. The skilled trades require years of hands-on training, specific apprenticeships, and physical endurance that a mid-career office worker simply doesn’t have. Also, flooding the trade unions with millions of desperate former middle-managers would crash the wages of actual plumbers and carpenters within a decade.

Corporations will hide behind nonsensical phrases like “human in the loop” to calm nervous shareholders and regulators. That single human in the loop turns out to be a lonely supervisor monitoring software that replaced 20 former colleagues. The output remains identical, the head count drops by 95 percent, and the corporate public relations team claims that nobody was truly replaced because a human still clicks the final button.

The final insult is the onboarding process itself. Companies routinely pay senior staff to document their daily processes, upload their work histories, and correct errors generated by automated tools. Employees spend six months carefully feeding their institutional knowledge directly into the system designed to make their positions redundant. They actively build their own replacements while waiting for an annual bonus that will never arrive.

If this economic trajectory feels slightly uncomfortable, it should, and the broader timeline offers even less comfort. Computer scientists at major research institutions place the probability of AI causing human extinction at somewhere around 10 percent . Either the algorithms gradually siphon off our paychecks until we end up living in glorified shipping containers, or the entire network achieves superintelligence and reduces the planet to a pile of irradiated ash.

We seem caught between a slow slide into economic irrelevance and rapid, absolute annihilation. Critics may call this hyperbole , but only the most deluded could look at where society is headed and feel confident about the future.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Trump posts poll to rename ‘AI,’ says current name is ‘inaccurate, and very ineloquent’
articles.summary: President Trump posted a poll on Truth Social, pitching potential new names for artificial intelligence — calling the emerging technology’s name “inaccurate.” In a Saturday Truth Social post, the president floated alternative names for AI — pitching “Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence.” He then asked his followers to vote on “which is the…
articles.body:
President Trump posted a poll on Truth Social, pitching potential new names for artificial intelligence — calling the emerging technology’s name “inaccurate.”

In a Saturday Truth Social post , the president floated alternative names for AI — pitching “Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence.” He then asked his followers to vote on “which is the best name for this ever growing ‘Revolution.'”

“Many people think that the words ‘Artificial Intelligence’ are inaccurate, and very ineloquent, relative to AI, or Artificial Intelligence,” he wrote.

These new names, Trump said, are a “far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena.”

As of 12:45 p.m. Saturday, over 27,000 users already weighed in with their opinion on Trump’s proposed alternatives.

The post comes as some Republican members of Congress split with Trump over his defense of the AI industry, and multiple tech CEOs — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Elon Musk, of Tesla and Space X — call for its development to slow.

Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Jon Husted (R-Ohio) both launched efforts this week to mitigate AI development concerns — namely surrounding data security and development of data centers.

On Thursday, Husted pushed legislation to compel tech companies to cover some of the costs of data center infrastructure. A day later, Hawley invited the CEOs of top AI-powered license plate reader manufacturers, such as Flock Safety, to testify before the Senate’s Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism as part of an investigation into the devices.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) took a middle ground stance on AI regulation — telling reporters Sunday, “Obviously, there’s a need for guardrails, but there’s also a keen need for the industry to self-regulate and self-monitor and report to us.”

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post . “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

Trump previously floated renaming AI to “supreme intelligence” in late 2025 , but he said at the time that the decision was up to industry leaders.

The president has also repeatedly defended AI and the emerging industry surrounding it; he has also forged close relationships with prominent tech moguls — some of whom will reportedly join Trump during a White House state dinner next week hosting Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

In one post, Trump called AI technology “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History,” saying it surpassed oil, gold and diamonds in terms of fostering development.

A Sept. 14 post from the president stated there was no real need for further regulation of AI, going against lawmakers’ calls for guardrails, at least so long as he is at the helm.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” the president wrote .

articles.title: A ‘ban on the free press’: White House bars journalists from three outlets
articles.summary: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico were denied access to White House on Saturday.
articles.body:
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico have been barred from entering the White House and have had their press credentials deactivated or confiscated, as United States President Donald Trump’s ban on the three news organisations took effect.

Journalists were turned away from the grounds on Saturday after Trump announced on Friday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House, accusing the outlets of reporting what he called “fake news”. Trump has said other outlets could also face bans.

CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein and MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner both reported on air that they had been denied access. Gardner said an officer confiscated her badge after telling her it had been disabled and that the decision was “above him”. An MS NOW photographer also had their badge disabled, she said.

Politico reporter Cheyenne Haslett was subsequently turned away, with Politico saying the Secret Service denied her entry and confiscated her White House access pass.

“A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter,” the news organisation said. “Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House.”

“We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House,” Politico added. “As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.”

“The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS NOW said in a statement. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”’

CNN media analyst Brian Stelter called the move “a direct threat to press freedom in the United States”.

“It’s so much bigger than CNN,” Stelter said. “This is a free speech test in America.”

The White House Correspondents’ Association said Trump had described “his own planned action as a ‘ban on the free press’”, and said constitutional press protections do not depend on whether a president approves of a news organisation’s coverage.

The ban is the latest in a series of confrontations Trump has had with news organisations during his first and second term.

In 2025, his administration restricted Associated Press access to the Oval Office and presidential travel after the agency declined to adopt the administration’s preferred name, “Gulf of America”, for the Gulf of Mexico. That case remains ongoing.

A key precedent is a 1977 federal appeals court ruling, Sherrill v Knight. The court found that once the White House establishes press facilities for credentialed journalists, access cannot be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons. It also said journalists denied credentials must receive notice of the factual basis, an opportunity to respond, and a final written explanation.

It is not yet clear what legal recourse CNN, MS NOW or Politico may pursue, or how courts would apply Sherrill to the administration’s decision to revoke existing credentials.

Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher reported from Washington, DC, on Friday that Trump’s ban will likely be challenged soon.

“The United States has the First Amendment [of its Constitution] that says the government cannot restrict access to this sort of thing,” he said.

Press freedom advocates are watching closely.

Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said in a news release that the move raises constitutional concerns.

“If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints,” Jaffer said.

The fight over access could now become a broader test of the limits on the White House’s ability to control which journalists can cover the administration.

“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. “It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move.”

articles.title: 60 years of the Animal Welfare Act and dogs are still suffering
articles.summary: ASPCA senior vice president Nancy Perry argues that Congress must pass Goldie’s Act to address the USDA’s chronic failure to enforce the Animal Welfare Act and protect dogs from systemic abuse.
articles.body:
We recently marked 60 years since the enactment of the Animal Welfare Act — landmark federal legislation that requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture to license and oversee commercial dog breeders who produce puppies to be sold wholesale to the pet trade, pet stores or research labs. Congress passed the law in response to public outrage over the horrifying conditions under which dog dealers were housing animals.

Yet six decades later, the cruelty persists. Although the recent removal of dozens of dogs from an Iowa puppy mill has been hailed as a victory for animal welfare, it is just further proof of the agency’s chronic failure to protect the animals it’ has been charged with overseeing.

The federal government should prevent these horrific outcomes, not allow animals to continue in these conditions for months if not years.

The Department of Agriculture licensed Iowa breeder Wuanita Swedlund three years ago. In the time since, the agency documented dogs at her facility suffering from untreated illnesses, painful injuries, and a lack of basic care, leading to multiple deaths. But the department chose to do nothing. It did not fine her, remove any dogs, or take her license away.

Finally, after she spent more than a year evading required inspections, officials entered her property and found even more appalling conditions . Dogs were emaciated, covered in fleas, and kept in filthy cages without clean food or water. But it was local law enforcement who removed more than 30 animals and placed them with a local shelter, and it was the county that charged Swedlund with 34 counts of animal neglect — not the Department of Agriculture.

The federal government has a responsibility to take action before a situation gets this far. Instead, it allowed repeated violations and inspection-dodging, leaving dogs to suffer and die for years in a facility for which it has direct oversight. And this wasn’t the first time.

More than 1,500 dogs were recently purchased by animal welfare organizations from federal licensee Ridglan Farms, which faced allegations such as performing eye operations on dogs without anesthesia or pain relief. While Wisconsin inspectors cited the facility for 494 state violations in a year , the feds only logged four Animal Welfare Act violations over the course of a decade.

Similarly, in 2022, federal licensee Envigo had thousands of dogs removed after the Department of Agriculture had documented years of severe abuse. This included euthanizing dogs via heart injection without the required anesthesia, resulting in an unnecessarily painful process.

And in 2021, hundreds of dogs were rescued from another licensed dog breeding facility in Iowa, operated by Daniel Gingerich . Gingerich kept his license for two years, even though the department had documented more than 100 American Welfare Act violations and a dog died in an inspector’s hands.

In all of these cases, dogs suffered for years, while federal regulators failed to protect them, leaving it to local law enforcement, shelters, or rescues to utilize their limited resources to remove, care, rehabilitate, and rehome the animals.

This is a systemic problem. The Agriculture Department is endowed with the responsibility to protect animals and the authority to revoke licenses, to remove suffering animals and to fine violators. Instead, it has long prioritized an excessively lenient policy focused on “educating” dog dealers in lieu of enforcing the law, leading to tremendous suffering and completely avoidable deaths.

A report by the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals found that, last year alone, the Agriculture Department had documented 680 instances where licensed dog dealers failed to meet the minimum standards of care, yet not a single violator lost its license.

Although the department has announced what seemed like a promising interagency effort to prioritize animal welfare, the department continues not to exercise the appropriate enforcement it is currently afforded under the law.

Congress must step in. The bipartisan Goldie’s Act would ensure that the department conducts meaningful inspections of these licensed facilities, addresses every violation, and intervenes to protect suffering animals.

Sixty years on, the Animal Welfare Act’s promise to protect vulnerable animals continues to elude us. By passing Goldie’s Act, Congress has the opportunity to fulfill the law’s intention and ensure these animals have the protections they are owed.

Nancy Perry is senior vice president of government relations for the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals .

articles.summary: Ohio’s gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races are neck and neck in new polling released this week. The Bowling Green State University (BGSU) survey found the Democratic candidates in these races hold 3-point leads over their GOP opponents among likely voters in the state. However, when asked about who is most likely to win, the Republicans…
articles.body:
Ohio’s gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races are neck and neck in new polling released this week.

The Bowling Green State University (BGSU) survey found the Democratic candidates in these races hold 3-point leads over their GOP opponents among likely voters in the state. However, when asked about who is most likely to win, the Republicans had the advantage.

In the gubernatorial race, 48 percent of likely voters backed Democratic nominee Amy Acton and 45 percent supported Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy. Sixty-two percent of those polled said they believe Ramaswamy will ultimately win the November contest.

Incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) also fell behind his Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, by three points, but 53 percent or respondents said the Republican will likely beat Brown in the midterm election.

The results in this new poll are similar to the outcomes in a June survey from AARP, which found the GOP candidates narrowly trailing behind their Democratic opponents.

Additionally, the BGSU survey asked respondents about the measure on the November ballot about whether to amend the state’s constitution to require voter ID — an issue that 66 percent of respondents said they had only heard between “some” and “nothing at all” about.

The proposed amendment is similar to President Trump’s “ Safeguard American Voter Eligibility ” (SAVE) Act, and it would require voters to present government-issued identification when going to cast their ballot.

Sixty-four percent of those polled on this issue said they would support this amendment, while 29 percent were against this change and 7 percent said they were “unsure.”

The survey also polled likely voters about their views on how Trump has handled his job as president. Sixty percent disapproved, with 49 percent expressing strong dissatisfaction with his job performance.

Robert Alexander, a BGSU political science professor, said the poll’s findings indicate Ohio voters are “becoming increasingly uneasy” about the president and the direction of the country and economy.

“Given that midterm elections are largely about the president’s approval, Democrats are poised to be competitive in a state Republicans have dominated electorally for two decades,” Alexander said in a statement .

The Bowling Green State University poll surveyed a sample of 1,000 likely Ohio voters between Sept. 1-10 with a margin of error of approximately 4 percentage points.
